group.passage: Sweet, sour, salty and bitter were long thought to be the only basic tastes. Text A tells how a Japanese chemist identified a fifth one more than a century ago, and in Text B, a taste scientist explains why the rest of the world was so slow to come round.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: The Secret in the Soup
passage_parts.text: In 1908, Kikunae Ikeda, a chemistry professor in Tokyo, set out to explain a puzzling flavor in dashi, a clear soup stock made from kombu seaweed. The taste was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter, yet it was clearly there, and Ikeda was determined to find its source. Working with a large amount of dried kombu, he extracted crystals of glutamate, a substance that is found in many protein-rich foods. He named the taste umami, from a Japanese word for “delicious,” and soon began selling the substance as a seasoning. A few years later, his student Shintaro Kodama found a second substance with the same taste in dried bonito flakes, the other main ingredient of dashi. In Europe and America, however, many scientists resisted the idea. Because these substances taste rather weak on their own, the new taste was often dismissed as nothing more than a “flavor enhancer.”

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Ask a Taste Scientist
passage_parts.text: People often ask me why umami took so long to be accepted. Part of the answer is that for most of the twentieth century, it was the odd one out. Textbooks listed four basic tastes, and most researchers felt that a fifth would simply be one too many. What finally changed their minds was the tongue itself. Around 2000, scientists discovered special receptors on our taste cells that respond to glutamate, much as other receptors respond to sugar. Once there was a receptor, there was a taste. Umami also makes good biological sense. Glutamate is the most common building block of proteins, so a liking for it would have steered our ancestors toward nourishing food. Babies even seem to be born ready for it, since breast milk is about as rich in glutamate as kombu dashi. These days, when cooks talk about the umami in tomatoes, mushrooms or aged cheese, nobody laughs at them any longer.

translation_zh.text:
甜、酸、鹹、苦長久以來被認為是僅有的幾種基本味覺。Text A 講述一位日本化學家如何在一百多年前找出第五種味覺；Text B 則由一位味覺科學家說明，為什麼世界其他地方這麼晚才接受它。

A｜湯裡的祕密
1908 年，東京的化學教授池田菊苗著手解釋高湯（dashi）裡一種令人困惑的味道；這種清澈的高湯是用昆布熬成的。這種味道不甜、不酸、不鹹也不苦，卻確實存在，池田決心找出它的來源。他用大量的乾昆布，萃取出麩胺酸的結晶；許多富含蛋白質的食物裡都有這種物質。他根據日文裡「好吃」的說法，把這種味道命名為 umami（鮮味），不久就開始把這種物質當成調味料販售。幾年後，他的學生兒玉新太郎在高湯的另一種主要材料柴魚片裡，找到第二種具有同樣味道的物質。然而在歐洲和美國，許多科學家抗拒這個想法。因為這些物質單獨吃時味道相當淡，這種新味覺常被貶為不過是一種「增味劑」。

B｜請問味覺科學家
常有人問我，為什麼鮮味花了這麼久才被接受。部分原因是，在二十世紀的大部分時間裡，它都是格格不入的那一個。教科書列出四種基本味覺，大多數研究者覺得再加上第五種就太多了。最後改變他們想法的是舌頭本身。2000 年前後，科學家在我們的味覺細胞上發現了會對麩胺酸起反應的特殊受器，就像其他受器會對糖起反應一樣。有了受器，就有了味覺。從生物學的角度看，鮮味也很合理。麩胺酸是蛋白質最常見的組成單位，所以喜歡這種味道，會引導我們的祖先去找有營養的食物。嬰兒甚至似乎一出生就準備好接受它，因為母乳所含的麩胺酸，和昆布高湯差不多豐富。如今，當廚師談起番茄、蘑菇或熟成起司裡的鮮味時，再也沒有人會笑他們了。
